summary: Maintain the k-th largest element as numbers stream in.
mainInsight: You only ever need the k largest values: keep them in a min-heap of size k whose root is the k-th largest; a new value matters only if it beats the root.
invariant: Between calls the heap holds the k largest values seen so far (all of them if fewer than k have arrived); its root, the minimum, is the k-th largest.

approaches.name: Sort on every add
approaches.timeComplexity: O(n log n) per add (O(n) on nearly sorted)
approaches.interviewRelevance: A fine first brute force; interviewers expect you to move on to the heap.

approaches.name: Min-heap of size k
approaches.summary: Push, pop when size > k; root = k-th largest.

personalSolution.approach: Min-heap of size k (heapify the initial list, then trim to k)
personalSolution.timeComplexity: O(n + (n - k) log n) to build, O(log k) per add
personalSolution.notes: Optimal per add. Trimming with heappop costs (n - k) log n in __init__; feeding each initial number through add instead costs n log k.

commonMistakes: Using a max-heap, which needs all n items or k pops per query
Forgetting to pop after the push, so the heap keeps growing and heap[0] is the minimum of everything
Reading heap[-k] on a heapq list, which is not sorted
Keeping an extra list of every number, which defeats the O(k) memory
edgeCases: Initial list shorter than k, or empty
k = 1: the answer is the running maximum
Duplicates each occupy a slot in the heap

promptVariants: Which technique solves this problem, and what in the statement or constraints points to it?

cards.answer: Min-heap of size k whose root is the k-th largest, updated on every add. Clue: It asks for the k-th largest repeatedly while values keep arriving, so keep only the k largest seen so far with the smallest of them on top.
keyPoints: It asks for the k-th largest repeatedly while values keep arriving, so keep only the k largest seen so far with the smallest of them on top.
cards.explanation: The k-th largest is the smallest of the top k, so a min-heap of size k exposes it at the root and a new value only matters if it beats the root.

rubric.technique: Min-heap of size k whose root is the k-th largest, updated on every add

alsoValid.name: Append and sort after every add

promptVariants: Which structure maintains the k-th largest of a stream?
What data structure gives O(log k) per update?
options: Stack of the k latest values
cards.explanation: The root of a size-k min-heap is the smallest of the k largest values, i.e. the k-th largest.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Max-heap holding all n items: Reading the k-th largest would take k pops, and all n values must be stored.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Sorted array rebuilt per add: Rebuilding costs O(n log n) per add, and inserting in place costs O(n).
incorrectOptionExplanations.Stack of the k latest values: A stack orders by arrival, not by value, so the k-th largest is not at an end.

promptVariants: Why use a MIN-heap, not a max-heap, to track the k LARGEST values? Say what the root represents and why the rest can be discarded.
Why can every value below the current k-th largest be thrown away, and why does that make a min-heap of size k the right tool?
cards.answer: The value that would be displaced next is the smallest of the current top k, so it must sit at the root: it is the k-th largest, and it is the one to pop when the size exceeds k. Values smaller than the k-th largest can never become the k-th largest later, because new values only push the threshold up, so they can be discarded.
keyPoints: Root = smallest of the top k, which is the k-th largest
Threshold only increases, so smaller values never matter again
Pop the minimum when the size exceeds k
cards.explanation: Hence O(k) memory and O(log k) per add. A max-heap would put the largest value at the root, which is the one we never need to evict.

promptVariants: After every call to add, what exactly does the heap contain, and what does heap[0] represent?
State the invariant that holds for the heap between two calls to add.
cards.answer: The heap holds the k largest values seen so far (every value, if fewer than k have arrived). Its minimum, heap[0], is therefore the k-th largest.
keyPoints: Contains the k largest values seen so far
heap[0] is the minimum, i.e. the k-th largest
With fewer than k values it holds all of them
cards.explanation: Push-then-pop-if-too-big preserves this invariant on every add.

promptVariants: Why does add push the new value first and only then pop when the size exceeds k?
What is the point of the push-then-pop order in add?
options: One pop then evicts the true smallest of the k + 1
heappush is O(1), so it must run before any pop
heappop on a heap with k items raises an error
heapq allows pushes only before the first pop
cards.answer: One pop then evicts the true smallest of the k + 1
cards.explanation: After the push the heap holds the k old values plus the new one; popping the minimum removes whichever of those k + 1 is smallest, whether or not it is the new value.

incorrectOptionExplanations.heappush is O(1), so it must run before: heappush is O(log k), and its cost does not decide the order.
incorrectOptionExplanations.heappop on a heap with k items raises an: heappop only raises on an empty heap.
incorrectOptionExplanations.heapq allows pushes only before the firs: heapq allows any mix of pushes and pops.

promptVariants: This __init__ heapifies a copy of nums and pops while the heap is larger than k. Why does that leave exactly the k largest values, and how does its cost compare with calling add once per initial number?
Explain what the while loop in __init__ does, why the result is correct, and what the construction costs.
cards.answer: Each heappop removes the current minimum, so after n - k pops the k largest values remain with the smallest of them at the root. Cost: heapify is O(n) and each of the n - k pops is O(log n), so O(n + (n - k) log n). Feeding every initial number through add keeps the heap at size k and costs O(n log k), which has the smaller log factor when k is much smaller than n.
keyPoints: Popping the minimum n - k times leaves the k largest
O(n + (n - k) log n) versus O(n log k) via add
cards.explanation: Neither choice changes the per-add cost of O(log k).

promptVariants: What if the initial array has fewer than k elements?
How does the heap version behave until k elements exist?
options: It keeps every value until k exist; nothing is popped yet
It raises an error because the heap has fewer than k items
It returns 0 for every query until the heap holds k values
It pads the heap with -inf values until its size reaches k
cards.answer: It keeps every value until k exist; nothing is popped yet
cards.explanation: The problem guarantees at least k elements when add is called, so heap[0] is valid; before that nothing is popped.

promptVariants: With k = 1 and an empty starting list, what do add(-3), add(-7) and add(5) return, in order?
For KthLargest(1, []), what are the results of add(-3), add(-7), add(5)?
cards.explanation: With k = 1 the heap holds one value, the running maximum: -3, then -3 (the pushed -7 is the one popped), then 5.

incorrectOptionExplanations.-3, -7, 5: That returns the newest value, ignoring the larger earlier one.
incorrectOptionExplanations.-3, -7, -7: That tracks the running minimum, not the maximum.
incorrectOptionExplanations.-3, -3, -3: That never lets a larger value replace the root.

cards.explanation: One push and possibly one pop on a heap of size k.

promptVariants: What does the size-k heap store, how much memory is that, and why is discarding every other value safe?
Compare the memory of the size-k heap with keeping every number seen.
cards.answer: The heap stores only the k largest values seen, so O(k) memory instead of O(n) for every value. It is enough because a value outside the top k can never become the k-th largest later: the stream only adds values, so the k-th largest never decreases.
keyPoints: Values outside the top k can never matter again
cards.explanation: The k-th largest only moves up as values arrive, so discarded values stay irrelevant. Building from the initial list can briefly hold all n of them before trimming to k.

promptVariants: Two simpler designs are appending and sorting on every add, or keeping a sorted list with bisect.insort. What does each cost per add, and why does the size-k heap beat both?
Why is a size-k heap better than re-sorting the list, or inserting into a sorted list, on every add?
cards.answer: Append and sort costs O(n log n) per add (Timsort is near-linear on almost-sorted data, but still O(n)) and stores all n values. bisect.insort finds the spot in O(log n), but shifting the list makes the insert O(n). The size-k heap does one push and at most one pop, O(log k), and stores only k values.
keyPoints: Sort per add: O(n log n)
Heap: O(log k) time and O(k) space
cards.explanation: Interviewers often probe both brute forces before the heap; know why each loses.

promptVariants: Your add appends and sorts the whole list. What is the cost and how would a size-k heap change `__init__` and `add`?
Rewrite add with heapq.
cards.code:
def add(self, val):
    self.heap.append(val)
    self.heap.sort()
    return self.heap[-self.k]
cards.answer: Sorting costs O(n log n) per call (Timsort is nearly linear on almost-sorted data but still O(n)). With a heap: __init__ heapifies and pops until size <= k; add does heappush(val) and, if len > k, heappop(), then returns heap[0].
keyPoints: Sort per add is O(n log n)
push, pop if > k, return heap[0]
cards.explanation: The list called `heap` is not actually a heap in that code - naming matters.
